newsitem.title: CYPRUS: FEATURE - Derelict Cyprus village seeks new lease of life.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Derelict Cyprus village seeks new lease of life.

text.p: The elementary school at the end of a potholed path is bolted shut, its playground grotesquely overgrown.
The children have long gone. A rusted sign hanging over the entrance bears a slogan from Kemal Ataturk, founder of modern Turkey.
Somebody has sneaked in through a hole in the fence and drawn the blue-and-white Greek flag on a classroom blackboard.
Androlykou, on the remote northwestern tip of Cyprus, was one of several villages Turkish Cypriots left following Turkey's occupation of the northern third of the island in 1974.

Literally meaning "cave of the wolves", Androlykou was abandoned to the elements when its residents left it in 1975 -- and to a few hundred goats, sheep, chickens and dogs that have run riot ever since.
Rolling green hills dotted with almond trees offer a breathtaking view of the spectacular coastline, and on a clear day the distant mountains of Turkey.
"It looks like a cloud but it is always there," said Ioannis Taliotis, pointing to a tiny white speck. "That is the snow on the Taurus Mountains."

Now some of the derelict homes, temporarily administered by a department in the Cyprus Interior Ministry, have been leased to locals on condition that they be returned to their Turkish Cypriot owners should they decide to come back.
"We are asking the state for basic things," said Taliotis, a local Greek Cypriot doctor who has leased a home in the village. "We want electricity, water, telephone and a road."
The group of would-be residents, numbering some 30 people, hopes to get permission to form a local authority and start rebuilding the village.
POPULATION DWINDLES TO THREE

Over 25 years, the population of Androlykou, located on the edge of the rugged Akamas peninsula, dwindled from more than 600 to just three people -- a Turkish Cypriot with his Greek Cypriot wife and another elderly woman. The couple's children have left and are now living in towns.
And since 1975, time has stood still in the village built on the ruins of Mycenaean tombs. Legend has it that a buried treasure lies somewhere in the hills above the hamlet.

"It is supposed to be a golden pig with her piglets," chuckled Esgul Mustafa, 28, a farmer. "Nobody has ever found it," he added wryly, flicking a glance at the ramshackle stone building his parents Hassan and Hambou call home.
Gaping cracks in the wall caused by two earthquakes in the Paphos district in 1995 and 1996 have not been repaired, Taliotis said.

Some sandstone homes have been reduced to piles of rubble, others have had their outer bricks removed for use on other structures. The crescent and star -- Turkey's flag -- is still visible in faded white paint on the walls of some buildings.
Greek Cypriot Hambou, now 74, her Turkish Cypriot husband Hassan, 61, and their four children jumped off the United Nations truck taking them and their co-villagers north in 1975.

Hambou and Hassan stayed in Androlykou, with all the hardships that went with it. Many of the others settled in Myrtou, a village in the north that Greek Cypriot residents were forced to flee during the Turkish invasion.
ATTEMPT TO BREATHE NEW LIFE INTO VILLAGE
An unused electricity generator lies in the yard of Hambou and Hassan's home with a sheet of plastic over it. It powers the electronic milking machine for the goats and sheep.
Hassan and Hambou are used to coping without the luxury of having electricity at the flick of a switch. They don't need a phone either. That disappeared from the village square five years ago.

"This village epitomises everything happening in Cyprus... the heart of the island and the problems that go with it," mused Greek Cypriot Michalis Himarides, a farmer who leased a cottage at Androlykou two years ago.
"It would be great for the Turkish Cypriots to come back. That would be the ideal solution to the Cyprus problem and we would gladly give back their homes," he said.
Living conditions are hard. Hassan and Hambou are out most of the day with their flock.

Christina Pournouxouzi, a 78-year-old Greek Cypriot, lives on the other side of the village in a tiny room. She sits by a stable door staring out at her concrete-covered yard. She is lame and never leaves the room.
SON RETURNS TO HELP AGED PARENTS
Esgul, who lives in the western coastal town of Paphos, makes the 60 km (37 mile) trek through the mountains at dawn and dusk to help his elderly parents handle their herd of 500 goats and sheep.
He left Androlykou when he was 25.
"It wasn't much of a life," he says. "I was working until I dropped and I would start over again the next morning."
Now married with two children, returning to Androlykou in its present state is even harder.
"I've got two babies, where am I going to bring them?," Esgul said. "If there was electricity up here of course I would come."

Most of Androlykou's other residents seem happy enough. A large grey goat lounges on a ledge above the entrance of one building as a sheep and her young lamb stare inquisitively at strangers from the kitchen of a deserted mudbrick house. Pigs grunt from behind a faded yellow door of another home.
The blackened floors of most homes sound hollow.
"It's the layers of animal dung," Taliotis volunteered.
